Great news! The package `wcwidth` is [officially supported](https://pyodide.org/en/stable/usage/packages-in-pyodide.html) in the latest Pyodide release used by PyScript.

To use it in PyScript simply add it to the `packages` section of your TOML configuration like this:

```
packages = ["wcwidth" ]
```

Or if you're using a JSON configuration, like this:

```
{
    packages: ["wcwidth"]
 }
```

Read more about using packages in PyScript [in our documentation](https://docs.pyscript.net/latest/user-guide/configuration/#packages).

summary: Measures the displayed width of unicode strings in a terminal

examples.title: Measuring Widths
examples.code:
""" Measuring the *displayed* width of unicode strings. Python's built-in `len()` counts codepoints, but a terminal cell can be 1 cell wide ('a'), 2 cells wide ('中'), or 0 cells wide (combining marks like the accent in 'cafe\u0301'). The `wcwidth` package gives you the real on-screen width. Docs: https://wcwidth.readthedocs.io/ """ from IPython.core.display import display, HTML import wcwidth heading("len() vs. wcswidth()") note( "Compare Python's len() against " "wcwidth.wcswidth() for a few tricky strings." ) samples = [ "hello", # plain ASCII "コンニチハ", # Japanese, each char is 2 cells "cafe\u0301", # 'café' as 'e' + combining acute (4 codepoints, 4 cells) "\U0001F1FF\U0001F1FC", # 🇿🇼 regional indicator flag (2 codepoints, 2 cells) "♀\ufe0f", # ♀️ with VS-16 (2 codepoints, 2 cells) ] rows = ["stringreprlen()wcswidth()"] for s in samples: rows.append( f"{s}{repr(s)}" f"{len(s)}{wcwidth.wcswidth(s)}" ) display(HTML("" + "".join(rows) + "
"), append=True) heading("Single-codepoint widths with wcwidth()") note( "wcwidth.wcwidth() returns the width of one codepoint: " "0 for combining marks, 1 for narrow, 2 for wide, and -1 for control codes." ) for ch, label in [ ("a", "Latin 'a'"), ("中", "CJK 'middle'"), ("\u0301", "combining acute accent"), ("\n", "newline (control code)"), ]: note(f"{label} ({repr(ch)}): width = {wcwidth.wcwidth(ch)}")

examples.title: Aligned Table
examples.code:
# Aligning a table of mixed-width text. # # `str.ljust()` pads to a number of *codepoints*, which produces ragged # columns when the data contains wide CJK characters or combining marks. # `wcwidth.ljust()` and friends pad to a number of *display cells*, # which is what your eyes (and a monospace terminal) actually care about. heading("A menu in three languages") note( "Each row has a dish name and a price. We'll render the menu twice: " "first with the standard library's str.ljust(), then with " "wcwidth.ljust()." ) menu = [ ("Espresso", "$3.00"), ("コーヒー", "¥400"), ("café au lait", "€4.50"), ("绿茶", "¥25"), ("Pão de queijo", "R$8"), ] # Naive alignment using str.ljust on codepoints -- columns will be ragged. naive_lines = [f"{name.ljust(16)} {price}" for name, price in menu] # Width-aware alignment using wcwidth.ljust on display cells. aware_lines = [f"{wcwidth.ljust(name, 16)} {price}" for name, price in menu] display(HTML( "

str.ljust() (ragged):

" f"
{chr(10).join(naive_lines)}
" "

wcwidth.ljust() (aligned):

" f"
{chr(10).join(aware_lines)}
" ), append=True) heading("Centering and right-justifying") note( "wcwidth.center() and wcwidth.rjust() are " "drop-in replacements for the string methods of the same name." ) banner_width = 24 for title in ["Menu", "メニュー", "café"]: centered = wcwidth.center(title, banner_width, "*") display(HTML(f"
{centered}
"), append=True)

examples.title: Wrap Clip Sequences
examples.code: # Working with text that contains terminal escape sequences. # # Real terminal output is often littered with ANSI color codes ("SGR"), # hyperlinks, and cursor movement. wcwidth knows how to measure, wrap, # clip, and strip these sequences without breaking them. heading("Measuring text that contains ANSI color codes") note( "wcwidth.width() understands escape sequences and " "reports only the cells that will actually be drawn." ) colored = "\x1b[1;31mERROR\x1b[0m: disk full" note(f"Raw repr: {repr(colored)}") note(f"len() says {len(colored)} codepoints.") note(f"wcswidth() says {wcwidth.wcswidth(colored)} (-1 means it gave up on control codes).") note(f"width() says {wcwidth.width(colored)} visible cells.") heading("Stripping escape sequences") note( "strip_sequences() removes all terminal escapes, " "leaving plain text." ) plain = wcwidth.strip_sequences(colored) note(f"Stripped: {repr(plain)}") heading("Wrapping text to a column width") note( "wrap() respects grapheme clusters and wide characters, " "and propagates SGR styles across line breaks so colors don't leak." ) paragraph = ( "\x1b[36mThe quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog.\x1b[0m " "コンニチハ、世界。 cafe\u0301 latte." ) for line in wcwidth.wrap(paragraph, 20): note(f"{repr(line)}") heading("Clipping by display column") note( "clip(text, start, end) extracts a substring by visible " "column positions, splitting wide characters cleanly with a fill." ) cjk = "中文字幕" # 4 wide chars = 8 cells note(f"Original: {cjk} ({wcwidth.wcswidth(cjk)} cells)") note(f"clip(0, 3): {wcwidth.clip(cjk, 0, 3)} (wide char split, padded with space)") note(f"clip(1, 5, fillchar='.'): {wcwidth.clip(cjk, 1, 5, fillchar='.')}") heading("Iterating over grapheme clusters") note( "A user-perceived character ('grapheme') may span several codepoints. " "iter_graphemes() yields one cluster at a time." ) family = "ok\U0001F468\u200D\U0001F469\u200D\U0001F467" # 'ok' + 👨‍👩‍👧 clusters = list(wcwidth.iter_graphemes(family)) note(f"Input has {len(family)} codepoints but only {len(clusters)} graphemes:") for g in clusters: note(f"  {repr(g)} width={wcwidth.wcswidth(g)}")
